papers.title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
papers.abstract: How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor. We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).

papers.title: A Spectral Renormalization-Group View of Learning
papers.abstract: We study how the layers in deep neural networks (NNs) converge, using Wilsonian Renormalization-Group (RG) ideas to organize the spectral picture. During training, these layers often develop heavy-tailed power-law (PL) spectra, and the strongest checkpoints often appear near the PL exponent $\alpha\approx 2$. This pattern raises a simple question: why should this value mark a well-trained layer? The answer is both statistical and physical. Our statistical hypothesis is that $\alpha=2$ marks the boundary between stable if not optimal learning and overfitting via non-self-averaging. The physical answer is that the same value makes the spectral energy gain scale evenly across logarithmic spectral scales, which is the proposed Wilsonian marginal condition. We then apply the ERG trace-log condition, the proposed SETOL theory, which we justify by taking volume-preserving, scale-invariant transformations to remove arbitrary layer scale along the proposed RG flow. The resulting spectral RG flow connects the HTSR and SETOL theories to optimizers such as Muon, and motivates a new optimizer extension, WW-PGD. Together, these results point toward a spectral Renormalization-Group view of learning, in which NNs may approach shared spectral structure in the settings studied here.

papers.title: Embedding stochastic dynamics in latent manifolds of recurrent neural networks
papers.abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a theoretical framework for understanding computation in biological neural circuits through their ability to support rich time-dependent behaviour. Whilst high-dimensional by construction, they can be used to encode low-dimensional dynamical systems, for example by restricting to low-rank connectivity, hence mirroring the emergence of latent neural manifolds found in empirical neural data. Here, we exploit a relationship between RNNs and a class of universal approximators to train networks that can represent arbitrary, nonlinear stochastic differential equations (SDEs), with given drift and diffusion coefficients, within a low-dimensional latent subspace. We show that RNNs can faithfully embed the drift and diffusion of a given SDE, including nonlinear and nonequilibrium dynamics such as chaotic attractors. We apply this approach by constructing RNN realisations of stochastic systems that transiently explore various attractors through both input-driven switching and autonomous transitions driven by nonequilibrium currents, which we interpret as models of associative and sequential (episodic) memory. To elucidate how these dynamics are encoded in the network, we introduce decompositions of the RNN based on its asymmetric connectivity and its time-irreversibility. Our results show that neural populations can implement a broad class of stochastic dynamics within low-dimensional manifolds, unifying ideas from the dynamics of neural computation, the theory of neural manifolds, associative memory, and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.

papers.title: Synchronization transitions in Kuramoto oscillators with mixed interactions
papers.abstract: The Kuramoto model is a paradigmatic system for emergent synchronization phenomena, and significant efforts have been made to investigate its transition from incoherent to coherent dynamics. However, previous studies have almost exclusively assumed global coupling between the oscillators, even though many real-world systems are organized in specific network structures. Here, we fill this gap by examining finite-size effects in Kuramoto oscillator ensembles on networks with mixed-order interactions. Using numerical simulations, we show how parameters such as the size of the system, the average degree of the nodes and the strength of the interactions alter the behaviour of the transition to synchronization with respect to the known theoretical results that are derived for globally coupled infinite systems.

papers.title: Slow structures, fast degrees of freedom, and the morphology of chess openings
papers.abstract: Chess openings naturally separate into slow and fast degrees of freedom: pawns evolve through irreversible moves, whereas pieces can be rapidly reorganized within the resulting structure. We exploit this separation to construct a quantitative morphology of opening space. From a catalogue of 3810 named variations, 1749 reach a common depth of $N=10$ plies, corresponding to 619 distinct positions and only 435 joint pawn structures. We characterize these positions through observables measuring pawn commitment and spatial organization, blockade and tension, and piece activity and centralization. Their partial independence reveals a multidimensional opening space and in order to explore its structural organization, we construct a network whose nodes are distinct White pawn structures, connected when a single pawn move or capture transforms one into another. Remarkably, 139 of the 149 observed structures belong to a single connected component containing $98\%$ of all positions. This network exhibits a statistically significant modular organization, with eight communities whose representative structures correspond to familiar pawn formations. Rather than forming isolated categories, these formations emerge as distinct regions of a connected structural landscape. Our approach thus complements the traditional opening taxonomy by revealing similarities between differently named openings and providing a quantitative basis for comparing the positions they produce.

papers.title: Imprints of information scrambling on eigenstates of a quantum chaotic system
papers.abstract: How are the spatial and temporal patterns of information scrambling in locally interacting quantum many-body systems imprinted on the eigenstates of the system's time-evolution operator? We address this question by identifying statistical correlations among sets of minimally four eigenstates that provide a unified framework for various measures of information scrambling. These include operator mutual information and operator entanglement entropy of the time-evolution operator, as well as more conventional diagnostics such as two-point dynamical correlations and out-of-time-ordered correlators. We demonstrate this framework by deriving exact results for eigenstate correlations in a minimal model of quantum chaos -- Floquet dual-unitary circuits. These results reveal not only the butterfly effect and the information lightcone, but also finer structures of scrambling within the lightcone. Our work thus shows how the eigenstates of a chaotic system can encode the full spatiotemporal anatomy of quantum chaos, going beyond the descriptions offered by random matrix theory and the eigenstate thermalisation hypothesis.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of the equilibrium Kauzmann transition in a two-dimensional atomistic glass
papers.abstract: Dense liquids gradually transform into non-equilibrium amorphous solids as they pass through the experimental glass transition. Experimentally, ergodicity is lost because measurements are conducted within a finite time window. More than seventy years ago, Kauzmann posed a fundamental question: If experiments could run indefinitely, would there exist a critical temperature at which an ergodicity-breaking phase transition occurs? Random first-order transitions represent the modern theoretical framework for this idea. However, theoretical calculations in finite dimensions are challenging, whereas experimental and numerical limitations on accessible timescales hinder direct observation of the putative Kauzmann transition. Here, we overcome this longstanding barrier by developing a computational strategy that properly combines three Monte Carlo methods to access the desired equilibrium thermodynamic properties of a two-dimensional atomistic glass-former down to zero temperature across a range of system sizes up to 77 particles. This enables us to directly measure thermodynamic and structural observables that provide unambiguous evidence that the system undergoes a finite-size version of the Kauzmann transition at a temperature that is much lower than other energy scales and decreases rapidly with system size, thus suggesting the existence of a zero-temperature Kauzmann transition for two-dimensional glasses. The transition is towards an ideal glass state characterized by a complex energy landscape and a hierarchical organization of low-lying states.

papers.title: A Machine Learning study of the two-dimensional antiferromagnetic $Q$-state Potts model on the square lattice
papers.abstract: The critical phenomena of 2D antiferromagnetic $Q$-state Potts model on the square lattice with $Q=2,3,4,5$ and 6 are investigated using supervised neural networks (NN). Conventional supervised and unsupervised NNs either fail or have difficulty in identifying the correct critical behaviors of these models. Remarkably, despite the fact that the NNs employed here are trained with a particular fixed type training set which contains no information about the considered models (except for $Q=2$), they correctly compute the critical temperatures for the studied physical systems. Particularly, the NN outcomes suggest convincingly that the $Q=3$ model is critical only at zero temperature and $Q=4,5,6$ models remain disordered at all temperatures. Apart from the studied models, our NNs trained with exactly the same training set have successfully determined the critical temperature(s) and the nature of the associated phase transition(s) of another physical system differing dramatically from those considered here. Therefore, our NN has the potential to be a universally applicable NN model in studying phase transitions.

papers.title: Feedback percolation on complex networks
papers.abstract: Traditional percolation theory assumes static microscopic rules, limiting its ability to describe real-world complex systems where macroscopic order actively regulates local interactions. Here, we introduce feedback percolation, an unified framework that dynamically couples the microscopic activation probability to the macroscopic size of the giant component. We show that this simple feedback mechanism produces a rich variety of behaviors both analytically and numerically. Depending on the feedback functions, the system exhibits explosive discontinuous jumps, hybrid transitions, limit-cycle oscillations, and routes to chaos, absent in classical percolation. Our findings establish that macroscopic feedback provides a unifying physical mechanism for phenomena ranging from self-regulating oscillations to systemic infrastructure collapse.

papers.title: Distinct mechanisms underlying in-context learning in transformers
papers.abstract: Modern distributed networks, notably transformers, acquire a remarkable ability (termed `in-context learning') to adapt their computation to input statistics, such that a fixed network can be applied to data from a broad range of systems. Here, we provide a complete mechanistic characterization of this behavior in transformers trained on a finite set $S$ of discrete Markov chains. The transformer displays four algorithmic phases, characterized by whether the network memorizes and generalizes, and whether it uses 1-point or 2-point statistics. We show that the four phases are implemented by multi-layer subcircuits that exemplify two qualitatively distinct mechanisms for implementing context-adaptive computations. Minimal models isolate the key features of both motifs. Memorization and generalization phases are delineated by two boundaries that depend on data diversity, $K = |S|$. The first ($K_1^\ast$) is set by a kinetic competition between subcircuits and the second ($K_2^\ast$) is set by a representational bottleneck. A symmetry-constrained theory of a transformer's training dynamics explains the sharp transition from 1-point to 2-point generalization and identifies key features of the loss landscape that allow the network to generalize. Put together, we show that transformers develop distinct subcircuits to implement in-context learning and identify conditions that favor certain mechanisms over others.

papers.title: Predicting accurate solid-state thermodynamics is easier than you think
papers.abstract: Materials underpin modern technologies, from energy harvesting, storage, and conversion to information and communication technologies. Their functionality is often governed by the interplay between competing phases, and thermodynamic behavior shapes microscopic properties and ultimately determines technological performance; for instance, the light absorption of inorganic metal-halide perovskites in solar cells. Accurately predicting crystal thermodynamics, however, remains a major challenge for computational approaches because strong anharmonic effects require extensive sampling of the potential energy surface. Here, we present an on-the-fly Bayesian framework, combined with the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation, for learning first-principles potentials. This approach enables the prediction of thermodynamic properties over a broad temperature range with first-principles accuracy while requiring training on only a few atomic configurations. A relevant finding is that the majority of the required structures are obtained from a single inexpensive dataset generation step, demonstrating that the relevant physics for accurately predicting solid-state thermodynamics is encoded in a few physically meaningful configurations. We investigate the thermodynamic and dynamical properties of Li$_2$O, $\alpha$--CsPbI$_3$, and $\delta$--CsPbI$_3$, requiring only 44, 256, and 50 total-energy calculations, respectively. Notably, we show that this framework accurately captures the extreme thermal expansion of \ce{Li2O}, and the phase diagram of CsPbI$_3$ with a predicted transition temperature within 20 K of experiment. More broadly, the method presented opens an interesting route toward accelerated materials engineering under realistic conditions for a wide range of technologically relevant applications, including batteries, photovoltaics, and memristors.

papers.title: Time evolution in the multi-component dynamical Keldysh models
papers.abstract: We construct a time evolution operator for a dynamical quantum models with a multi-component random Gaussian field characterized by a long correlation time. We analyze three paradigmatic cases: non-Abelian $SU(2)$ symmetry class for the three-component Gaussian noise and Abelian symmetry classes $U(1)$ and $Z_2$ for the two- and one-component noises correspondingly. Starting with a limiting case of the infinite correlation time (Keldysh model) we shown that statistics of the two-component random field with a non-zero mean is described by the Rice distribution. We derived and solved the system of coupled linear differential equations for the exact diagonal and off-diagonal single-particle Green's functions. We showed how the finite time correlation in Keldysh models are accounted by a continuous fractions method.
